runs.text: Ditos, ou graças que hum diz no Za

lines.note: Kyoutai denotes entertaining remarks or witticisms at a gathering. The scan and the preceding page's catchword support Qeôtai rather than OCR Deǒeu; Ditos, graças, and no also replace garbled OCR. Za begins the Japanese room-name within the Portuguese sentence and shares its printed italic type, confirmed on the second pass.

runs.text: xiqui, ou conuite, &c. pera entreter os hoſpe-

lines.note: Za plus xiqui forms zashiki, the room or gathering where the remarks are made. The Japanese continuation remains in the surrounding italic font; the Portuguese explains a banquet and entertaining the guests, with hospedes divided after hoſpe-.
The example means uttering entertaining remarks. Qeôtaiuo is a complete upright Japanese word, correcting the OCR's italic O and truncated beginning.
Completes apraziveis pera entreter, pleasant things said to entertain. This closes the opening entry.

The two Japanese expressions denote dawn or the early morning. The alternative begins with long ſ, giving ſǒten rather than OCR fôten; its o mark is a worn caron, not a circumflex; the gloss's polama- continues below.

Completes pola manhaa cedo, early in the morning. Here enlargement places the tilde over the first a, agreeing with the supplied nhãa. This local reading is retained despite the reference sheet's warning that earlier audited pages generally have nhaã; the scan, not that distribution, decides this occurrence.
Ashii itazuramono explains a bad or dissolute person. The double z in itazzuramono is retained, and the Portuguese description continues below.
The man is described as bad, lawless, and of evil habits. The scan reads singular deſaforado followed by de, not OCR deſaferados; Cu begins kuni on the next row without a printed hyphen.
Kuni no kyoutora means the dissolute people of the realm; -ra supplies the group sense. The translation divides vadios after va-.
Completes idle or dissolute people who are in the realm. Reyno is retained in its historical spelling.
Kyouoku concerns the breast or heart, explained by two mune glosses. The visible Qeôuocu corrects OCR Qebuocu, and the repeated example begins Qeô- rather than the OCR's italic O.
Qeô-uocu ni osamuru means placing or keeping something in one's breast or mind. The historical voſamuru remains as printed rather than being modernized.
The Portuguese completes the inward-storage metaphor as keeping something in the breast or heart.
Oshiyuru mono, one who teaches, is equated with shishou, a teacher. The visible space before mono is restored; Meſtre begins the Portuguese explanation.
The master teaches and gives advice. The damaged sequence supports dà auiſos rather than OCR dã zuiſos; the small accent is a grave in the chosen reading.
Mune no uchi identifies the inside of the breast. The printed comma after Qeôxi and period after i are retained, and S is an upright written-usage label.

Oshie nushi, the master of the teaching, is identified as Shaka or a Buddha. The Japanese names Xaca and Fotoque share the printed italic type of the explanatory ou, as confirmed at enlargement on the second pass; no independent accent can be established above the final u, so the OCR caron is removed. The supplied NINJAL lexical index also has unaccented Qeôxu, but the local scan is the authority (Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, v202510; NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima, Taichi Aida; CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html).
This entry is glossed as mixture. The headword's terminal comma is printed, and the written-usage S is upright.

runs.text: Exequias, ou com mendação que ſe faz

lines.note: The entry concerns funeral observances or a commendation for the dead. The scan preserves the close but visible division com mendação; it is not silently modernized to a modern technical term.
The rites are performed for a deceased person. Bumo kyouyou no begins the example about one's father and mother.
Tameni suru completes doing something for the parents' memorial observance. The Portuguese renders this as acting for their souls.
Completes 'of one's father and mother'. Pay and mãy retain their historical spelling and the mother's nasal mark.

runs.text: O estimar, ou fazer caſo. Vt,

lines.note: This distinct word concerns valuing or taking notice of something. The initial headword and divided example both lack an accent on their first o in the scan; the final yô is supplied on the next row.

runs.text: ¶ Item Modo de conſentir, ou tomar

lines.note: Qeoyô suru completes the first example; the second sense is assent or taking another's words well. The scan reads conſentir, not OCR conſemtir.
Completes taking well what another person says. This is the assent sense of the preceding entry, not a new expression.
Majiwaru tomo identifies a companion or associate. The scan gives a circumflex on the first o, correcting OCR Qeǒyu, and leaves final u unaccented despite an expected long vowel.
Completes companheiro, a companion. The following upright S is the written-usage label.
Warui nusubito explains an openly lawless thief. The scan restores initial Q, the i in Varui, and Portuguese Ladrão in place of the OCR's oeôzocu, Varu, and Fadrão.
Desaforado completes the description as lawless or unrestrained. This is not a separate action by the thief.
Keppaku is explained as purity or cleanness. Xǒ- begins the compound shoujou in the example continued below.
Shoujou keppakuna kokoro means a clean and pure heart. The row preserves the physical division of shoujou and the printed adjective form qeppacuna.
Puro completes the heart's description as pure. The short continuation closes the entry before the blood-oath term.

runs.text: Sinal que ſe faz ao modo

lines.note: Keppan and ketban are alternative names for a signed pledge sealed with blood. The visible b in qetban corrects OCR qetan.

runs.text: de Iapão pera prometer, ou jurar algũa couſa

lines.note: The sign is made in the Japanese manner to promise or swear something. The scan separates ou jurar, unlike the OCR's joined sequence; Iapão is Portuguese and remains italic.

runs.text: pondolhe em cima algũa gota do ſeu ſangue.

lines.note: A drop of the signer's blood is placed on the mark. The scan reads pondolhe, correcting pendo lhe without modernizing the historical attached pronoun.

Musubi fuuzuru explains tying and sealing. The visible caron is restored in fǔzuru; Portuguese mutrar and mutra below are retained as the dictionary's sealing vocabulary rather than replaced with modern selar.

runs.text: Mutrar, ou por mutra em cou-

lines.note: Qeppu wo nasu means applying the seal. The Portuguese explains placing a mutra on a bound object and divides cousa after cou-.
Completes the sealed object's description as tied and fastened. Està retains its grave accent.
Hana and konomi identify flower and fruit, matching the Portuguese pair. Upright S is a usage label rather than part of fruito.
Kera is identified only as an insect of that name. The note does not impose a precise species beyond the source's brief definition.

Keraku concerns pleasant enjoyment, matching alegria and contentment below. The headword clearly has r, not OCR t. Cecoroyoi is retained as the locally abraded printed reading; kokoroyoi is the likely intended Japanese word, but its expected o is not silently substituted for the uncertain e.
Contentamentos completes the definition as joy or satisfactions. Its plural form is preserved.
Kerai denotes a household or its people. The scan reads Familia rather than OCR Familla; Qe- begins the following Japanese example and is upright throughout.
Kerai no mono denotes household people or servants. The printed close setting oucriados is retained, and fami- continues familiares below.

Liares completes familiares de alguma casa, members or dependants of a household. The visible continuation is indented like the preceding row, correcting its missing indentation metadata as well as OCR ltures.
Kerikeri is identified as a bird of that name. The initial is Q, not OCR D; the rest of the short zoological gloss is retained without a modern species assignment.

runs.text: Hum certo ornato como cordoẽs com bor-

lines.note: Kesa is described here as an ornament resembling cords with tassels. Bor- continues into borlas at the top of Column 2; this is a cross-column body continuation, not a catchword.

runs.text: las que os Bonzos trazem ſobre o vestido.

lines.note: Bor-las completes the tassels of the preceding column's kesa definition. The gloss says that bonzes wear this ornament over their clothing.

This separate kesa means this morning, not the religious garment. The scan's tilde sits over the first a in menhãa; the supplied spelling is retained rather than forced to the more usual nhaã pattern described in the reference notes.
The entry denotes an obstruction, and the example means creating one. The repeated word is contiguous, correcting OCR Q eſaſauo; Fa- begins fazer.
Completes making an impediment or obstruction. Both Portuguese nouns explain the same Japanese example.

runs.text: Regra com que ſe deitão linhas, ou

lines.note: Kesan is a ruler used for drawing lines. The scan supplies the t in deitão, lost by the OCR, and does not support a space inside the headword.
Completes making ruled marks or strokes. This is the ruler's function, not a new headword.
Kari no sugata, a provisional form, is glossed as the human body. The short s in Qesǒ and long ſ in ſugata are retained as locally printed.
Kessai denotes cleanness or purification through abstinence. The definition continues with the foods avoided.

runs.text: de comer carne, & peixe como custumão fazer

lines.note: The abstinence consists of not eating meat or fish, following the practice attributed to bonzes below. Historical custumão is retained.
The example begins 'today is a day of abstinence and purification'. Two long-s types are visible in qeſſaini, restoring the second one omitted by the OCR.

runs.text: Oje he dia de purificação não comẽ

lines.note: Gozaru completes the Japanese statement. The Portuguese explains today's purification and begins comendo with a nasal abbreviation, without a visible line-end hyphen.
Completes not eating fish or meat, then begins the corresponding verb phrase. The repeated qeſſai again has two long-s types, not the OCR's single one.
Ru completes suru. The Portuguese describes performing this abstinence and purification.
The checked-final form Qet is illustrated by kessuru, to determine, and explained by sadameru. The visible mixed ſs in Qeſsuru is retained rather than harmonized with the next row's ſſ.
Ri wo kessuru concerns deciding the merits or principle of a matter. The gloss permits investigation or giving judgment, completed below.
Completes passing judgment on a dispute. This explains the legal application of the determination verb.

runs.text: Pao comprido que poem ſobre as colum-

lines.note: Keta is a long structural beam laid over columns. Colum- continues the Portuguese noun on the following row.

runs.text: nas, & depois em cima deste pao os aguieiros.

lines.note: The rafters are then placed on top of this beam. Aguieiros is the printed construction vocabulary and is not modernized.

runs.text: Couſa graue, alta, ou nobre. Vt,

lines.note: Kedakai denotes dignity, elevation, or nobility. Vt introduces examples involving a house and a person.

Kedakai ie and hito mean a noble house or person. The scan appears to print bomem, as in the supplied baseline, rather than expected homem; that apparent printing anomaly is preserved with this caveat.
Noble and dignified complete the description. The scan reads graue, correcting OCR groue while preserving u for v.
Kedakasa is the corresponding abstract noun, dignity or nobility. Its unglossed short row belongs to the preceding adjective family.
Kedakou is the associated adverbial form. Italic Adu. is the grammatical label, not part of the Japanese form.
Kari no tai, a provisional body, is again glossed as the human body. The final upright S labels written usage.

Qetate, with its conjugational endings tçuru and eta, means raising something by kicking it. The Portuguese infinitive Aleuantar starts the definition, which continues on the next physical row; the abbreviation over algũa is retained.

The definition specifies doing this with the foot, then gives Focoriuo qetatçuru, raising dust by kicking. The Portuguese translation begins with the separate line-final A-; it must remain here rather than be joined graphically to the following row.

runs.text: leuantar pò com os pees. ¶ Per met.

lines.note: This completes Aleuantar and the dust example, then introduces a metaphorical use. The Japanese example begins with Za-, continued as xiqiuo on the next row; the entire Japanese fragment, including its printed hyphen, is roman rather than partly italic.

Together with Za- above, xiqiuo gives zashiki as the object of qetatçuru: leaving or rising from the gathering in anger. Zaxi- is a Japanese noun embedded in the Portuguese explanation and shares its printed italic type; its final qui belongs to the following physical row, so neither fragment is offered as a whole-word typeface term.

The opening qui completes the italic Japanese Zaxi- from the preceding row. The Portuguese qualification says that the departure is passionate or disorderly; the nasal abbreviation cõ is not expanded to modern com.

runs.text: Qetban. Muſubi tçugǒ. i, Banno xidai.

lines.note: This Qetban entry concerns an order or rotation of watch duty, as Banno xidai and the following Portuguese explanation establish. The accidental OCR space inside the headword is removed; tçugǒ retains its visible caron. Or continues as dem below without adding an unprinted hyphen.

runs.text: dem que ha no vigiar. ¶ Item, Faltar na

lines.note: Dem completes Ordem, the order governing watch duty. After the paragraph mark, a second sense begins: failing to take one's assigned watch; the comma after Item and the physical break after na are retained.

runs.text: vigia que lhe cabe por ordem.

lines.note: This completes the second sense: missing the watch that falls to a person in the rotation. The initial vigia belongs to the preceding Faltar na, not to a new headword or independent entry.

The second Qetban is a blood signature, explicitly paraphrased as Chino fan. The Portuguese says signed in blood; the existing ß representation in Aßinado and long ſ in ſangue are retained rather than systematically regularized.

Qetbanuo ſuyuru supplies the act of affixing the blood signature. The scan has the reflexive infinitive Aſinarſe, including the r omitted by the draft; the Portuguese ſan- continues into gue on the next row.

runs.text: gue. i, Pondo ſobre ſeu ſinal eſcrito com tin-

lines.note: The broken word ſangue is completed and the method is explained: putting blood on a signature written with ink. The explanatory i, remains within the printed italic Portuguese, and tin- is the beginning of tinta rather than Japanese material.

runs.text: ta algũa gota de ſeu ſangue. Vide,

lines.note: This completes tinta and specifies a drop of the signer's own blood. The roman cross-reference Qeppan points back to the related entry in the left column; the OCR's internal Q eppan space is not supported by the word setting.

Qetbocu is deficiency or want, with Caquru and toboxij as Japanese explanatory equivalents. The Portuguese ne- starts necessario across the line boundary; the double i spelling of toboxij is not modernized.

Ceßario completes the definition and Fiǒrǒga qetbocu xita illustrates provisions running short. Both carons in Fiǒrǒ are visible and retained; Fal- is the printed beginning of the Portuguese translation on the next row.

This completes Faltarão os mantimentos, the translation of the shortage-of-provisions example. The historical spelling and nasal ending are transcribed as printed rather than adjusted to a modern tense interpretation.
Qetdan is a decision or determination, paraphrased as settling a judgment. Dancǒuo has the printed caron and ſadamuru the long ſ; the Portuguese Determi- continues physically into nação below.

runs.text: nação, ou aſſento de muitos juntos.

lines.note: The completed Portuguese definition describes a determination or resolution by several people together. The scan reads muitos, not the draft's maitos; the two long-ſ characters in aſſento are preserved.

Qetgue concerns the summer observance or retreat, literally paraphrased by Natçuuo muſubu. The Portuguese reads eſtio, including the narrow i lost by OCR, and begins a calendrical explanation continued on the following two rows.

runs.text: que he des dos oito da quarta lũa ate o meyo

lines.note: The summer period is reckoned from the eighth day of the fourth lunar month to the midpoint specified below. Des dos, lũa, ate and meyo are the historical printed forms; no modern accent or contraction is supplied.

This completes the calendrical endpoint, the middle of the seventh lunar month. The short continuation remains a separate indented body row, and the nasal mark over the u of lũa is retained despite wear.

Qetguan is making a vow, with Negaiuo muſubu as the Japanese paraphrase. The Portuguese noun vo- continues as to on the next physical row; the headword's gu sequence is not confused with the preceding Qetgue.

After completing voto, the example Qetguan jǒju ſuru describes fulfilling the vow. The caron in jǒju and the historical Portuguese Comprir are retained; the translation continues with its object below.

This finishes the example as fulfilling the vow already made. The complete text and final stop are above the bottom furniture, so the signature and catchword below are not continuations of this body row.
